ai.definition: Brain-Computer Interfaces for Cognitive Enhancement are non-invasive devices designed to read and stimulate brain activity to enhance mental capabilities such as cognitive performance and memory.
ai.howItWorks: These interfaces utilize neuroimaging techniques like EEG (Electroencephalography) and fMRI (Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging) to decode neural signals. The decoded signals are then used to provide feedback or stimulation, which can help improve cognitive functions.
ai.problemSolved: They address the need for non-invasive methods to enhance cognitive performance and memory without the risks associated with invasive procedures.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves creating devices that can accurately interpret brain activity using sensors and processing units. The process requires precision in sensor placement, material selection, and software development.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes designing the hardware components, integrating neuroimaging technology, programming algorithms for signal decoding, and testing the device's effectiveness and safety.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the high-quality sensors needed for accurate readings, complex processing units, and rigorous testing protocols. The cost of advanced neuroimaging technologies also plays a significant role.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is expected to enter the market in the near future as research continues to validate its effectiveness and safety.
ai.regulation: Regulations will likely involve approvals from health authorities, such as FDA (Food and Drug Administration) or CE marking for European markets, focusing on device safety and efficacy.
ai.risks: Risks include potential side effects from brain stimulation, ethical concerns about cognitive enhancement, and the need for continuous validation of effectiveness over time.
ai.profitability: Profitability will depend on market acceptance, pricing strategies, and reimbursement policies. Initial costs may be high but could decrease as technology matures.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development is expected to focus on improving accuracy and personalization of brain activity decoding, expanding the range of cognitive functions that can be enhanced, and addressing ethical concerns through clear guidelines and regulations.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking.

glossary.def: Electroencephalography, a technique that measures electrical activity in the brain using electrodes placed on the scalp.
Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging, a neuroimaging method that measures changes in blood flow associated with neural activity.

subsystems.name: Sensing front end
subsystems.role: measures brain activity, usually as tiny voltages on the scalp.

subsystems.name: Decoding pipeline
subsystems.role: turns noisy recordings into an estimate of the user's mental state.
parts: artefact rejection for blinks and muscle activity

subsystems.name: Stimulation stage
subsystems.role: nudges activity in a chosen brain region, or provides feedback only.
parts: or a TMS coil for deeper targets

subsystems.name: Closed-loop controller
subsystems.role: adjusts stimulation in real time based on the decoded state.

subsystems.name: Training task and interface
subsystems.role: the cognitive work the user does while the loop runs.

subsystems.name: Verification layer
subsystems.role: separates a real effect from expectation and practice.

buildSteps.title: Define the target and the outcome
buildSteps.detail: Choose a specific function such as working memory span or sustained attention, and a validated test that will measure it before and after.

buildSteps.title: Fit the sensor
buildSteps.detail: Place electrodes at standard scalp positions, check contact impedance, and record a baseline of the individual's brain activity at rest and during the task.

buildSteps.title: Train a personal decoder
buildSteps.detail: Collect many labelled trials, extract rhythm power and connectivity features, and fit a classifier that separates the mental states of interest.

buildSteps.title: Choose the stimulation dose
buildSteps.detail: Select electrode montage, current (typically 1–2 mA for tDCS, well under tissue-damage thresholds), duration and ramp-up, with a hardware limit that cannot be exceeded.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop
buildSteps.detail: Feed the decoded state back within tens of milliseconds to trigger stimulation or adapt the task, then iterate over multiple sessions.

buildSteps.title: Run controlled trials
buildSteps.detail: Compare real against sham stimulation in blinded participants, and test whether any gain transfers to untrained tasks and persists after the device is removed.

buildSteps.title: Harden the hardware
buildSteps.detail: Move from gel electrodes and lab amplifiers to dry arrays, automatic calibration and drift compensation so the device works outside a shielded room.

buildSteps.title: Clear a regulatory path
buildSteps.detail: Decide whether the product is a medical device for a clinical deficit or a lower-risk wellness product, and gather the safety data each route requires.

prerequisites.why: comfortable, long-wear sensors are needed for daily use, but signal quality still lags gel electrodes.
rhythm and state decoding is routine in laboratories; the gap is robustness outside the lab.

prerequisites.tech: Causal maps of stimulation to cognitive circuits
prerequisites.why: without knowing which circuit change produces which cognitive gain, dosing is guesswork.
skull thickness, anatomy and brain state all change how much current reaches a target region.
single sessions look safe, but years of repeated stimulation have not been studied.

pathway.milestone: neurofeedback and tDCS marketed for attention and memory; TMS used clinically for depression in several countries
pathway.unlocks: a large user base and cheap hardware, but weak and inconsistent evidence for enhancement in healthy people.

pathway.milestone: closed-loop systems that time stimulation to an individual's own brain rhythm
pathway.unlocks: effects larger and more reproducible than fixed-dose stimulation, because dose adapts to state.

pathway.milestone: implanted memory prostheses in small clinical trials, such as the DARPA Restoring Active Memory programme
pathway.unlocks: a ground-truth model of which signals matter, which can be approximated non-invasively.

pathway.milestone: individually calibrated devices with blinded, replicated evidence of durable cognitive gain
pathway.unlocks: legitimate clinical use for deficits and a defensible route to enhancement claims.
